segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So I, the prisoner in the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling with which you were called,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: making every effort to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were also called in the one hope of your calling;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: one Lord, one faith, one baptism;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But to each one of us grace was given according to the measure of Christ’s gift.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore it says:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “When he ascended on high, he led captives into captivity; he gave gifts to people.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now what does “he ascended” mean, except that he also descended to the lower parts of the earth?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The one who descended is himself also the one who ascended far above all the heavens, so that he might fill all things.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And it was he who gave some as apostles, others as prophets, others as evangelists, others as shepherds and teachers,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to equip the holy ones for the work of service, for building up the body of Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a full-grown man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that we may no longer be infants, tossed by the waves and carried about by every wind of teaching, through the trickery of people, through cunning that serves the scheming of error.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Instead, speaking the truth in love, we are to grow in every way into him who is the head, Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: from whom the whole body, fitted and held together by every supporting joint, as each single part works in its measure, makes the body grow so that it builds itself up in love.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So this I say and insist on in the Lord: you must no longer walk as the Gentiles also walk, in the futility of their minds.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They are darkened in their understanding, alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, because of the hardening of their hearts.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Having lost all feeling, they have given themselves over to debauchery, for the practice of every kind of impurity, with greed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But that is not how you learned Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: if indeed you heard him and were taught in him, just as truth is in Jesus,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to put off the old self that belongs to your former way of life and is being corrupted by the desires that come from deceit,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to be renewed in the spirit of your minds,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and to put on the new self, created in the likeness of God in the righteousness and holiness that come from the truth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore, having put off falsehood, each of you speak truth with your neighbor, because we are members of one another.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and do not give room to the devil.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let the one who steals steal no longer; rather let him toil, doing what is good with his own hands, so that he may have something to share with the one in need.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let no rotten word come out of your mouths, but only what is good for building up as the need requires, so that it may give grace to those who hear.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, with whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let all bitterness and rage and anger and shouting and slander be removed from you, along with all malice.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Be kind to one another, compassionate, forgiving each other just as God in Christ also forgave you.

notes.note: “Walk” is a Semitic idiom for how a person conducts their life, familiar from the Septuagint. Many modern translations paraphrase it as “live.” It is kept here because the image recurs through the letter (see verse 17).
“Meekness” now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes a person who is not harsh or self-assertive. “Gentleness” or “humility” is the mainstream modern rendering.

The quotation is from Psalm 68:18 (67:19 in the Septuagint), a psalm about God ascending in triumph. Both the Hebrew text and the Septuagint say that he “received gifts among people,” where Ephesians has “gave gifts to people.” A later Jewish Aramaic paraphrase of the psalm also reads “gave,” so the author may be following an existing line of interpretation, but how the wording arose is debated.

notes.phrase: the lower parts of the earth
notes.traditional: the lower parts of the earth
notes.note: The Greek can mean the regions beneath the earth, that is, the realm of the dead, or “the lower parts, namely the earth,” in which case the descent is Christ’s coming to earth. Early interpreters mostly took the first view; many modern scholars take the second, and a minority think of the Spirit’s descent after the ascension. The rendering leaves the question open, as the Greek does.

“Pastor” is the Latin word for shepherd and has since become the title of a church office. The Greek is the ordinary word for someone who tends a flock, used here as a picture of those who care for the community. “Shepherds and teachers” share a single article in Greek, which may indicate one group with two functions or two closely linked groups; this is disputed.

The word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. “Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people.”

This was an everyday word for service or for a task carried out on someone’s behalf, from waiting at table to delivering a commission. “Ministry” now suggests clergy or a church profession, which the Greek word did not. Most English translations use “ministry” here.

notes.phrase: to equip the holy ones for the work of service
notes.traditional: for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry
notes.note: Older translations took the three phrases of this verse as parallel, so that the leaders named in verse 11 themselves do the work of service. Most modern translations and scholars read it as here: the leaders equip the holy ones, and the holy ones do the work. The change of preposition in the Greek after the first phrase favors this, but the older reading still has defenders.

The adjective means complete or full-grown, not morally flawless, and is set against the “infants” of verse 14. The noun is singular and is the word for an adult male: the whole community is pictured growing up together into one mature figure. Many modern translations paraphrase as “mature manhood” or “maturity.”

The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples,” and in the plural it was the ordinary Jewish term for the non-Jewish peoples; English uses two words where Greek has one. The readers were themselves non-Jews by birth (2:11), so the term here marks a way of life they have left and not their ancestry.

The Greek is literally “the old human being,” set against “the new human being” of verse 24; the image is of taking off one garment and putting on another. Older translations have “the old man,” and “self” is the common modern rendering. Some interpreters hear a wider sense, an old humanity and the new humanity created in Christ (compare 2:15).

notes.phrase: Be angry and do not sin
notes.traditional: Be ye angry, and sin not
notes.note: The words reproduce Psalm 4:4 (4:5 in the Septuagint) without any introductory formula. The command “be angry” is usually understood as a concession, “if you are angry, do not sin,” and not as an instruction to be angry; some take it as permitting or even requiring anger at wrongdoing. The rendering keeps the form of the Greek.

candidates.reason: Recurs throughout Paul and John for moral conduct; translations split between “walk” and “live,” and the choice should be uniform so the recurring image is visible.
Recurs in Paul for the growth of the community; translations vary between “edification,” “building up” and “upbuilding,” which hides the construction metaphor.
The phrases “old/new ἄνθρωπος” recur in Romans 6:6, Ephesians 2:15 and Colossians 3:9–10, and “man,” “self,” “person” and “humanity” are all live options that should be decided once.
Appears in vice lists across the Gospels, Paul, Peter and Jude, where translations vary between “sensuality,” “licentiousness,” “debauchery” and “lewdness.”
A key term across Paul, Luke and Hebrews; “redemption” is traditional but some prefer “release” or “liberation,” so one decision is needed.
